title: Counting Intersections of a Parabola and an Exponential Curve
originalTopic: Number of intersection points found graphically and numerically
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
problemStatement: A graphing tool left on a small window suggests that y = x^2 and y = 2^x meet only once. Determine how many intersection points the two curves actually have and give their x-coordinates.

steps.title: Test the obvious exact solutions
steps.explanation: Substituting shows that x = 2 and x = 4 satisfy x^2 = 2^x exactly, giving two intersection points (2, 4) and (4, 16).
steps.why: Exact integer solutions anchor the count and reveal that the curves cross twice on the positive side, something a window ending near x = 3 hides.

steps.title: Search the negative side with a sign check
steps.explanation: Since g is continuous and changes sign between -1 and 0, a third crossing lies in that interval; numerical solving gives x approximately -0.767.
steps.why: The Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees a root in the bracket, so the extra intersection is real and not a plotting artifact.

steps.title: Confirm the total with growth comparison
steps.explanation: Exponential growth eventually dominates quadratic growth, so for x > 4 the curve y = 2^x stays above y = x^2 and no further crossing is possible; a window near [-3, 6] by [-1, 20] displays all three crossings.
steps.why: Comparing end behavior bounds the number of further intersections, turning a picture into a trustworthy count of three.
